name: Retries, Timeouts and Idempotency
question: Is it safe to try that again?
summary: Tool calls time out, drop connections and return 5xx errors. Reads can be retried freely. A write that moves money or sends a message needs an idempotency key, created once per logical action, so a retry returns the first result instead of repeating the action. Every call gets a timeout, and retries use capped exponential backoff with jitter. This technique makes one call safe to repeat; the AgentOps module covers protecting the whole system when a dependency keeps failing.
useCases: Tools that pay, refund, debit, book or send messages
Gateways and partner APIs that time out under load
Durable workflows that replay steps after a crash

items.detail: timeouts, 429 and 5xx; never a 4xx that will fail again
one per logical action, reused on every retry
store the first response per key; replay it; reject a changed payload
idempotentHint defaults to false, destructiveHint to true

steps: Label every tool as a read, an idempotent write or a non-idempotent write
Put a timeout on every call and retry only timeouts, 429 and 5xx
Back off exponentially with full jitter and a cap on attempts
Create the key once per action; have the server store and replay results by key
pitfalls: A fresh key on every attempt looks safe but repeats the action
Retrying in lockstep turns a brief outage into a retry storm
A lost response after success is the dangerous case: the action happened, the client does not know
remember: One action, one key, every retry.
caption: Illustrative UPI refund. The retry reuses key 7f3c, so the gateway replays the stored result.

comparison.needs: Medium: key store on the server

steps.title: Classify the tools
steps.text: Reads are always safe to retry. An idempotent write, such as setting a limit to ₹50,000, is safe too. A refund is a non-idempotent write: running it twice pays twice.

steps.title: Give every call a timeout
steps.text: The refund call waits at most 10 s. Without a timeout, a hung connection holds the agent’s turn for ever.

steps.title: Retry only what can succeed
steps.text: Timeouts, dropped connections, 429 and 5xx are worth another try. A 400 or 422 will fail the same way again, so it goes back to the model instead.

steps.title: Back off with full jitter
steps.text: Each retry waits a random time between zero and min(8 s, 0.5 s × 2^attempt), with at most 4 attempts, so clients that failed together do not retry together.

steps.title: Create the key once per action
steps.text: The key is derived from the dispute and stored, so every retry, and even a resumed agent, sends the same key for the same refund.

steps.title: Store and replay on the server
steps.text: The first request with a key runs and its response is stored for 24 hours. A repeat gets the stored response; a repeat with a different body gets 422.

pros: Retries become safe for payments, refunds and messages
Lost responses no longer cause duplicate actions
Backoff with jitter protects a recovering service
Works across agent restarts when the key is stored
cons: Needs a key store and replay logic on the server side
Keys must be scoped and expired correctly
Retries add latency to the slowest requests
Third-party APIs without key support need your own deduplication
avoidWhen: Pure reads, which are safe to retry without a key
Calls that must never be retried automatically, such as a trade the user must reconfirm

playgroundGuide.scenario: A payments support agent issues 100 UPI refunds of ₹2,499 through a gateway with a 10 s timeout. Some attempts fail. In the dangerous case the refund runs but the reply is lost, so the agent cannot tell success from failure. Retries back off from 0.5 s, doubling up to 8 s. Figures are expected values.
controls: Set the failure rate per attempt, and whether failures are lost responses (the refund ran) or failures before the refund.
Set the number of retries and the idempotency-key strategy.
Turn full jitter on or off.

outputs.meaning: Extra executions when a retry is not recognised as a repeat.

outputs.meaning: Retries arriving in the busiest 100 ms after an outage.

outputs.name: p95 time to a confirmed refund
outputs.meaning: Timeouts plus backoff waits for 95% of refunds to be confirmed.

presets.name: Retries, no key
presets.expect: 30% lost responses and 2 retries: 97% confirmed, but 39.0 extra refunds per 100 and a burst of 100 retries at once; p95 24.0 s.

presets.name: New key per attempt
presets.expect: Exactly as bad: 39.0 extra refunds per 100, because every attempt looks like a new refund to the gateway.

presets.name: One key per refund
presets.expect: The same retries with one key per refund: 0 duplicates. Still 97% confirmed and a burst of 100.

presets.name: Many retries, no jitter
presets.expect: 50% failures before the refund runs and 5 retries: no duplicates, 98% confirmed, but every retry wave hits at once (100) and p95 is 56.0 s.

missions.text: With at least 30% lost responses and 2 or more retries, get zero duplicate refunds.
missions.hint: The key must stay the same across every attempt of one refund.
At a 30% failure rate, 1 − 0.3^attempts must reach 0.99.

missions.text: Keep retrying, but hold the peak burst under 20 requests per 100 ms.
missions.hint: Full jitter spreads each retry wave over its backoff window.

tools.best: Retry decorators with exponential backoff, full jitter, stop rules and retry conditions.
tools.ex: Wrap the refund call in @retry with wait_random_exponential and stop_after_attempt(4).
pros: Works for sync and async code
cons: Easy to retry errors that will never succeed

tools.best: Seeing how a payments API stores the first response per key and rejects reused keys with new parameters.
tools.ex: Send Idempotency-Key with every refund request and reuse it on every retry.
cons: Keys can be pruned after 24 hours

tools.best: An idempotency decorator for Lambda handlers, backed by DynamoDB or other persistence layers.
tools.ex: @idempotent on a refund handler, keyed by a hash of the dispute id and amount.
pros: Stores and replays results for you

tools.best: Durable workflows where activities are retried automatically and must be idempotent.
tools.ex: A refund workflow retries the gateway activity with the workflow id as the idempotency key.
pros: Retries, timeouts and state survive crashes
cons: Significant platform to run or buy
Activities still need idempotent side effects

tools.best: Claiming an idempotency key atomically with an expiry, as the core of your own store.
tools.ex: SET idem:<key> running NX EX 86400 before calling the gateway.
cons: You build replay and payload checks yourself

quickPicks.need: Long-running flows that must survive crashes

goals: Classify tools by whether a retry is safe
Calculate expected duplicates from failure rate and retries

practice.scenario: An NBFC collections agent presents a NACH debit for an overdue EMI. The payment gateway times out at 10 s, but the debit had already gone through. Retried without a key, the borrower is debited twice. With one idempotency key per debit, reused on every retry, the gateway returns the stored result of the first attempt and nothing is charged again.

industries.use: Refunds, payouts and UPI collect requests keyed per business action
WhatsApp and SMS sends that must not reach a customer twice
Seat holds and bookings retried after a partner API timeout

practice.analogy: A cheque with a serial number. If the courier isn’t sure it arrived and you send a photocopy, the bank sees the same serial number and pays it once.

library.name: tenacity + httpx
library.what: tenacity adds retry rules, capped exponential backoff with full jitter and attempt limits; httpx gives per-call timeouts.

practice.note: The client and server halves of one pattern. do_refund stands for your own payment call.

numericDrill.question: 1,000 refunds. The gateway always executes the refund, but 30% of responses are lost on the way back, independently on each attempt. The client retries up to 2 times after a lost response, with no idempotency key. How many duplicate refunds do you expect?
numericDrill.answer: Every lost response triggers a retry that executes again. Second executions: 1,000 × 0.3 = 300. Third executions: 1,000 × 0.3 × 0.3 = 90. Expected duplicates 390. With one key per refund the gateway replays the first result and duplicates are 0.

interview.question: How do you make a payment tool safe for an agent to retry?
interview.answer: Classify it as a non-idempotent write. Create an idempotency key once per logical action, store it with the action, and send it on every attempt. The server records the first response per key and replays it on repeats, rejecting a reused key with a different payload. Add a timeout per call, and retry only timeouts, 429 and 5xx with capped exponential backoff and full jitter.

interview.question: Why add jitter to exponential backoff?
interview.answer: Without jitter, clients that failed together retry together, so the retry waves hit the recovering service at the same instants. Full jitter picks a random wait between zero and the capped exponential value, spreading retries out. AWS found it did less total client work than the alternatives it tested.

mistakes.mistake: Generating a new idempotency key inside the retry loop
mistakes.fix: Create the key once per action and reuse it on every attempt
Retry only timeouts, 429 and 5xx; fix 4xx errors instead

quiz.question: A refund call times out at 10 s but the refund had actually gone through. The agent retries without an idempotency key. What happens?
quiz.explanation: Without a key the gateway cannot tell the retry from a new refund.

quiz.question: Where should the idempotency key for a refund be created?
options: Inside the retry loop, fresh on each attempt
Once per logical refund, stored and reused on every attempt
By the model in its arguments each time
By the gateway after the first attempt
quiz.explanation: One action, one key, reused on every retry, even after a restart.

quiz.question: 1,000 refunds; 30% of responses are lost after the refund runs, independently per attempt. The client retries up to 2 times with no key. How many duplicate refunds are expected?
Stripe receives a repeat request with the same idempotency key but different parameters. What does it do?
options: Processes it as a new request
Returns an error, because the parameters differ
quiz.explanation: Stripe compares parameters and errors if a key is reused with different ones.

quiz.question: Which errors are generally worth retrying automatically?
quiz.explanation: Transient errors can succeed on retry; other 4xx errors need a change.

quiz.question: AWS’s full jitter formula for the wait before a retry is:
quiz.explanation: Full jitter picks a random wait between 0 and the capped exponential value.

quiz.question: With base 0.5 s and cap 8 s, what is the maximum full-jitter wait before attempt 4 (using 2^4)?
Which tools need an idempotency key before an agent may retry them? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Writes that move money or send messages repeat their side effect; a status read is safe to retry.

quiz.question: Each attempt fails 30% of the time independently. With 3 retries (4 attempts), what share of requests eventually succeed?
Stripe keys can be up to how many characters?
quiz.explanation: Stripe allows idempotency keys of up to 255 characters.

quiz.question: Under the IETF Idempotency-Key draft, what status suits a duplicate request that arrives while the first is still being processed?
quiz.explanation: The draft recommends 409 Conflict for a concurrent duplicate, and 422 for a reused key with a different payload.

quiz.question: A payout service shows retry storms after brief outages. Which changes help? Select all that apply.
options: Add full jitter to the backoff
Retry immediately in a tight loop
quiz.explanation: Jitter spreads retries; caps bound total load. Tight loops make storms worse.

quiz.question: In MCP tool annotations, what is the default value of destructiveHint?
quiz.explanation: destructiveHint defaults to true and idempotentHint to false, so hosts assume the worst.

quiz.question: Which statements about MCP annotations are true? Select all that apply.
options: Annotations from untrusted servers should be treated as untrusted
readOnlyHint guarantees the server cannot write
quiz.explanation: Hints default to the cautious values and are only hints, especially from untrusted servers.

quiz.question: Temporal’s documentation says what about business-logic Activities?
options: You should always make them idempotent
They run exactly once by design
quiz.explanation: “You should always make your business logic Activities idempotent,” because they may be retried.

quiz.question: A refund of ₹2,499 is duplicated for 39 out of every 100 customers across 1,000 refunds. How much is overpaid?
An idempotent write, such as setting a data cap to 10 GB, is retried after a timeout. What happens?
options: The end state is the same: 10 GB
quiz.explanation: Repeating an idempotent write leaves the same state.

quiz.question: How should a server implement idempotency keys? Select all that apply.
options: Claim the key atomically, for example with SET NX, before running the action
Store the first response and replay it for repeats with the same key
Generate a new key for each repeat
Delete the key as soon as the first response is sent
quiz.explanation: Atomic claim plus stored responses make repeats safe; new or deleted keys defeat the purpose.

quiz.question: The client times out while the server is still processing a charge. Which case is the dangerous one for duplicates?
options: The request never reached the server
The action succeeded but the response was lost
The client had no network at all
quiz.explanation: If the action happened but the client did not learn of it, a retry without a key repeats it.

quiz.question: Which tools provide retry or idempotency support? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: tenacity handles client retries, Powertools stores and replays results, Temporal retries idempotent activities.
